DESCRIPTION: Orbitline is a fictional local-first code editor that keeps typing instant while people and agents edit the same files.
ANNOUNCE_TEXT: Orbitline 0.9 brings shared sessions to every plan.
HERO_BODY: Orbitline keeps every keystroke ahead of the work around it, so people and agents can share one file without anyone waiting on the network.
HERO_NOTE: macOS · Linux · Windows — fictional product, illustrative content
VALUE_1_BODY: The render loop drains keystrokes before any background work, every frame.
VALUE_2_BODY: Every buffer is a CRDT, so collaborators merge edits without a central server.
VALUE_3_BODY: Files stay on your machine; sessions sync peer to peer when you invite someone.

FEATURES_TITLE: The editor stays out of the way
FEATURES_BODY: Fast at rest, fast under load, and quiet about it. Each part does one job well.
FEATURE_1_BODY: Invite a teammate or an agent into the buffer you are editing; everyone keeps their own cursor and undo history.

FEATURE_3_BODY: Diagnostics and completions arrive incrementally, without blocking a frame.
FEATURE_4_BODY: Typed, layered settings you can review in a pull request.
FEATURE_5_BODY: Keep editing on a train; edits merge the moment you reconnect.

WORKFLOW_TITLE: From solo to shared in three moves
WORKFLOW_BODY: Collaboration is a property of the buffer, not a separate mode.
STEP_1_BODY: Work alone as usual. Nothing is uploaded and nothing waits on a server.
STEP_2_BODY: Share a session link. Edits travel peer to peer and merge through the CRDT.
STEP_3_BODY: Each collaborator's changes stay attributable, so you can review them like a diff.

QUESTION_1: Does my code leave my machine?
ANSWER_1: Not unless you start a session. Sessions connect peers directly; the relay only helps them find each other.
QUESTION_2: Can an agent edit while I type?
ANSWER_2: Yes. An agent joins a session like any collaborator, and its edits merge through the same CRDT as yours.
QUESTION_3: What happens when two people edit the same line?
ANSWER_3: Both edits survive in a deterministic order, so every replica ends with the same text.
ANSWER_4: No. It is a fictional product used to demonstrate gridline-style.
